t: A Little-Known Teaching Strategy That Makes Learning Easier -learning-easier/
q: When you tell students that something is hard, when you label it as hard, then it becomes hard. It becomes exactly what you say it is.
Sadly, students who are behind academically are the most affected. The second they hear you say that something is difficult, they check out.
Just as calling something difficult makes it difficult, calling something doable makes it doable. In other words, if you pretend it’s easy, then it becomes easy.
Now, it's important to point out that the strategy only works if your instruction is up to snuff.
One of the secrets to great teaching, and galloping progress, is to guide your students from one success to the next, all day every day.

t: Why Strict, Fair, Compassionate Accountability Makes You Popular With Students y-makes-you-popular-with-students/
q: You see, when you consistently hold students accountable according to rules and expectations you lay out ahead of time, it makes you the most popular teacher at school.
So when students meet someone that actually does what they say they’re going to do, they can’t help but be affected.

Once you prove to your students that the agreed-upon consequences are the only consequences, and that you’re not going to lecture, scold, glare, admonish, or otherwise take their misbehavior personally, it frees them to truly enjoy your class.
This, in turn, safeguards your relationship with them. In fact, it makes their trust and belief in you, as well as your likability, even stronger.
You must enforce your consequences like a referee rather than a judge.
So that your students will not only never hold your faithful accountability against you. They’ll love you for it.

t: 5 Signs You've Lost Control Of Your Class (But Don't Know It)
q: It’s the scores of teachers who have lost control of their class but continue to plow forward.
Well, after coaching hundreds of teachers over the past couple of years, and asking this very question, I now know the answer: It’s because they don’t realize they’ve lost control.

If you feel you have no choice but to give instruction while your students are talking (because of the time and trouble it takes to get them quiet), then you have very little influence over their behavior.
If you find yourself repeating much of what you say, and reminding your students again and again about the same things, then you’ve effectively trained them to tune you out.
In well-run, well-behaved classrooms, the teacher focuses on delivering great lessons while the burden of listening and learning falls in toto onto the shoulders of students.
The notion that stress and frustration are just part of the job is a lie.

t: A Lovely, Silent, Well-Behaved Way To End Each Day ch-day/
q: This underscores the importance of starting your wind-down early, of giving yourself enough time to calmly get your students ready to go.
Focusing the mind on a single sound, movement, or thought has a unique way of calming excitability, restlessness, tension, and stress. In fact, it’s the basis behind the practice of meditation.
Sit up straight (or stand) and place your hand on your stomach as you expand on the inhale and contract on the exhale.
Have them relive that experience by visualizing it, savoring it, and remembering how it felt.
In this way, that brief time of stillness and reflection will become a calming touchstone your students look forward to every day.
